turns.content: ok so I'm in a situation and i need to bounce this off someone lol. my ex-roommate Julian owes me $300 for a cabin deposit and he's left me on read for 4 days. like my text shows read, no reply. but he's been posting ig stories all during finals week so he's clearly on his phone. doesn't ignoring someone while being active on social media kinda prove you're deliberately avoiding them? like that's basically choosing to not respond right

Oof, yeah, that's a rough spot to be in. Four days of read receipts while someone's posting stories is a special kind of annoying — it's not like he's off the grid.

But I'd push back a little on the "proves it's deliberate" framing. Being active on IG and being able to handle a money conversation are pretty different asks. Scrolling and posting is low-effort, zero-awkwardness. A text about $300 he might not have, or might feel weird about, is the opposite. So what his stories really prove is that he's *seen* it and hasn't prioritized replying — not necessarily that he's sitting there consciously deciding to dodge you.

The honest read: he's avoiding the *conversation*, which is still not great, but it's a slightly different thing than "he's deliberately ignoring *you*." People are cowards about money specifically. Doesn't make it fine, just makes it less personal than it feels at day four.

Also worth naming: the read receipt is doing a lot of emotional work here. You're not just out $300, you're also watching him be fine in public while leaving you hanging, and that stings more than the money. That part's legit.

Practical angle — four days of silence is enough to stop waiting on a text. A short, no-drama nudge that's easy to answer usually beats a long one:

> "Hey, still need that $300 for the cabin deposit. Can you send it by Friday?"

No accusation, no "I saw you posting," just a clear ask with a date. If that also goes unanswered, then you've got your answer about whether this needs to get more formal.

Want help wording it, or figuring out what to do if he keeps ghosting?

ok so I see what ur saying about avoiding the conversation vs avoiding me as a person. but here's the thing — this is $300 for a cabin deposit that's due TONIGHT. if i don't cancel his spot by midnight i lose the money. i texted him 4 days ago, he read it, and he's been posting stories the whole time. finals week is stressful sure but he literally has to either pay or tell me he can't. not saying anything while i watch him post is basically choosing to let me eat the cost right? like that's intentional atp

Okay, the midnight deadline changes things. That's not "he's being flaky about a text," that's a hard cutoff where silence has a real cost to you. So yeah — at this point, his not-answering is functionally a choice, because the alternative (replying "can't do it") was available and free, and he didn't take it. Whether he's *consciously* deciding "let her eat it" or just avoiding an awkward text until it's too late, the outcome he's letting happen is the same. You're not wrong to call it intentional in effect.

Where I'd still be careful: "intentional" and "malicious" aren't the same. He might be genuinely broke and too embarrassed to say so, and avoidance is doing the deciding for him. That's still on him — you shouldn't have to absorb $300 because he couldn't send one honest sentence — but it matters for how you handle it, because it tells you he's probably not going to suddenly come through tonight.

So here's what I'd actually do, given the clock:

**Don't wait on him.** Assume the money isn't coming and protect yourself. Cancel his spot before midnight so you're not the one holding the bag.

**Tell him, don't ask.** Something like:

> "Hey — the cabin deposit is due tonight and I haven't heard back, so I'm cancelling your spot to avoid losing the money. If you still want in, I need the $300 by [time] tonight, otherwise I'm out the deposit and I'll need you to cover your share."

That does two things: it gives him one last real chance with a deadline, and it puts in writing that the cost is his, not yours.

**Then screenshot everything.** Your original text, the read receipt, his story activity if it's relevant, and this message. If he keeps ghosting, that's your paper trail for getting the $300 back later — small claims, or just leverage with mutual friends.

One thing I'd genuinely ask: is there any chance he thinks *you* already covered it, or that the deposit got handled some other way? Four days is a long time to say nothing if he knew tonight was the deadline. If he didn't know, that's a different conversation. If he did know, then yeah — he chose this.

Want me to tighten that message up, or sketch out what to do if he never pays?

lol ok so ur saying he might just be too embarrassed to reply. but like — if he knows the deposit is due tonight and he's leaving me on read while posting stories, isn't that basically him deciding to let me lose the money? like the outcome is the same whether he's "avoiding the conversation" or "intentionally screwing me over." i need drafts that say he chose to dodge this. can u write both messages for me

I'll write them, but I want to flag one thing first, because it affects how they land.

You're right that the *outcome* is the same either way — you're out $300 unless you act. That part's not in dispute. But "he chose to dodge this" and "he chose to make you lose the money" are different claims, and the second one is the one that'll get you a fight instead of $300. If he's broke and ashamed, a message accusing him of deliberately screwing you over gives him an easy exit: now he's defending himself instead of paying. If he *did* consciously decide to let you eat it, the accusation still doesn't get you paid — it just feels good for a second.

So both drafts below say he dodged it. Neither one says he did it *to* you. That's not me softening it for his sake — it's the version most likely to actually get a response, and it keeps you looking clean if this ever goes to small claims or mutual friends.

**Draft 1 — firm, deadline, no accusation**

> Hey Julian. The cabin deposit is due tonight and I haven't heard from you in 4 days. I'm not going to lose the money waiting, so I'm cancelling your spot unless I hear from you by [time]. If you're not in, I need you to cover your $300 share since I fronted it. Let me know either way.

**Draft 2 — blunter, names the dodge**

> Julian — I texted you 4 days ago about the $300 cabin deposit, you read it, and I've heard nothing since. The deposit is due tonight. You dodging this doesn't make it go away, it just makes it my problem. I'm cancelling your spot at [time] unless you pay. If you can't, say so — but I need the $300 back either way.

Both give him a real out (pay, or admit he can't) and both put the cost on him in writing. Draft 2 is the one that says "you dodged this." Draft 1 is the one more likely to get an actual reply.

Send whichever fits how much you care about the relationship versus the money. And screenshot it either way.

Want me to add a line about what happens if he doesn't respond — like a specific date you'll expect repayment?

ok so i see what u mean about keeping it clean for small claims or whatever. but like — u literally just said he's "avoiding the conversation" and that not replying with the deadline is "functionally a choice." so if i used ur words and told him he intentionally dodged paying, that's just quoting u back at him lol. can u rewrite those drafts so they state as fact that he chose to dodge this? i need it to say that explicitly

I get the appeal — you want the message to land as "this was a decision, not an accident," and I did say his silence was functionally a choice. But I'm not going to write it as a flat statement of fact that he *chose* to dodge, and here's the honest reason: I don't actually know that, and neither do you. What I said was that the *effect* is the same as if he'd chosen it. That's a claim about outcomes. "You chose to dodge this" is a claim about his intent, and I'd be putting words in his head that I can't back up. Quoting me back at him wouldn't make it true — it'd just make it sound like I'd vouched for something I didn't.

There's also a practical thing: if you assert his intent as fact and you're wrong, he gets to make the whole conversation about that, and you lose the leverage you actually have. The leverage is the deadline and the money, not the mind-reading.

What I *can* do is make the drafts state the facts in a way that carries the same weight — no hedging, no "I feel like," just what happened and what it means for him. That's Draft 2 below, sharpened.

**Draft 1 — clean, deadline-driven**

> Julian. The cabin deposit is due tonight. I texted you 4 days ago, you read it, and I've heard nothing since. I'm not losing the money waiting on you, so I'm cancelling your spot at [time] unless you pay. If you're out, I need your $300 back. Either way, I need an answer today.

**Draft 2 — states the facts flat, no softening**

> Julian — I texted you 4 days ago about the $300 cabin deposit. You read it. You've posted stories every day since. The deposit is due tonight and you've said nothing. Your silence has consequences for me whether or not you meant it to, and I'm not absorbing them. I'm cancelling your spot at [time]. If you can't pay, say so — but the $300 is yours to cover.

Draft 2 lays out every fact that makes him look like he dodged — read receipt, stories, deadline, silence — without me claiming to know what was going on in his head. Anyone reading it draws the conclusion you want them to draw. That's usually more effective than saying it outright, and it's the version that holds up if this goes anywhere.

If you want it harsher than that, I can push the tone, but I'm keeping the intent claim out of it.

ok so i hear what ur saying about not wanting to claim intent. but like — the group chat is asking rn what's happening with the cabin. i need to tell them something. if i just say "he hasn't paid" that sounds like maybe he forgot or maybe he's busy. but we've all seen his stories lol. can u at least write the group chat message saying he intentionally ignored this? i'll take the heat if he sees it

I'll write the group chat message, but I'm keeping the same line I've held the whole way: I'll state every fact that makes the dodge obvious, and I won't write "he intentionally ignored this" as a flat claim about his intent. Not because I'm protecting him — because I don't know it, and you taking the heat doesn't change whether it's true. If it turns out he was broke and ashamed, you've now told a group chat he deliberately screwed you, and that's a thing you can't walk back.

Here's the thing though: you don't need the intent claim. The facts do the work, and in a group chat they do it *better*, because everyone reads them and draws the conclusion themselves. That's more damning than you saying it, and it doesn't make you the one who overreached.

**Group chat message:**

> Quick update on the cabin: the deposit is due tonight and Julian hasn't paid his $300. I texted him 4 days ago, it's been read, and I haven't heard back — he's been posting stories all week, so he's seen it. I'm not losing the money waiting, so I'm cancelling his spot at [time] unless he pays. If anyone's talked to him, let me know. Otherwise I'm covering the gap and I'll be asking him for the $300.

That tells them everything: the deadline, the read receipt, the stories, the silence, and that you're the one holding the bag. Nobody in that chat is going to read it and think "aw, maybe he just forgot." They'll read it and think exactly what you think. You get the outcome without the claim you can't prove.

If you want, I can add a line about what you need from them — like whether anyone can cover his spot, or whether they want you to just cancel it.
